title: Childhood Emotional Abuse, Emotional Neglect, and Inhibitory Control
short: Whether childhood emotional abuse and emotional neglect relate to inhibitory control in different ways.
description: This project asks whether experiences of emotional maltreatment in childhood are associated with differences in inhibitory control later in life. Emotional abuse and emotional neglect are forms of psychological maltreatment that do not necessarily involve physical harm, and are therefore often difficult for participants to identify and report.
Inhibitory control is treated here as a behavioral index rather than a clinical one: the capacity to withhold a prepared response, measured through reaction times and error rates on a Go/No-Go task.
researchQuestion: Do childhood emotional abuse and emotional neglect relate differently to inhibitory control in Indian emerging adults?
background: The project grew out of an interest in how early emotional experience is carried forward into adult functioning, specifically into the cognitive control processes required to withhold a prepared response and act against a dominant one.

Inhibitory control is examined behaviorally through a Go/No-Go paradigm, in which responding to a frequent go signal and withholding it on stop trials can be measured directly through response times and error rates.

The design is informed by the Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology, which treats childhood adversity as having at least two dimensions rather than one: threat, involving actual or threatened harm, and deprivation, involving the absence of expected cognitive, social and emotional input. Emotional abuse is treated here as threat-based, and emotional neglect as deprivation-based.

Previous findings have been inconsistent, which is partly a measurement problem. Most studies of maltreatment and executive function use emotionally neutral tasks, and most treat maltreatment as a single cumulative score. Distinguishing the forms of adversity, and testing inhibitory control under emotional distraction as well as neutral conditions, are the two changes this study is built around.
role: Study design, stimulus prevalidation, programming, analysis

method.participants: Target sample of 150 Indian participants aged 18–25.
method.measures: Traumatic Antecedents Questionnaire (TAQ) subscale scores; items prevalidated for cultural relevance.
method.stimuli: Emotional picture sets prevalidated for valence and arousal.
method.task: Emotional Go/No-Go task with positive, negative and neutral distractors. Performance is recorded as reaction time and accuracy.
